/glossary.t: No-Win-No-Fee Glossary: CFA, DBA, Contingency Fee, Cuota Litis | JuriMatch
/glossary.d: Plain-language definitions of no-win-no-fee terms: contingency fee, CFA, DBA, ATE insurance, litigation funding, cuota litis, Erfolgshonorar and more, plus a side-by-side comparison.

faq.q: What is No win, no fee?
faq.a: An arrangement where you do not pay your own lawyer's fees if the case is lost. If you win, the lawyer is paid from the result or recovers fees from the other side. Court fees, expert costs and the other side's costs may still apply, so read the agreement.

faq.q: What is Contingency fee?
faq.a: The lawyer's fee is a percentage of the money recovered and nothing is due if there is no recovery. The percentage, and whether expenses are deducted before or after it, is set in the written agreement and is limited by local rules in some places.

faq.q: What is Conditional fee agreement (CFA)?
faq.a: The lawyer charges normal fees only if you win, plus a success fee on top of those fees. The success fee cannot exceed 100% of the base costs, and in personal injury claims it is capped at 25% of certain damages.

faq.q: What is Damages-based agreement (DBA)?
faq.a: The lawyer takes a percentage of the damages you recover instead of hourly fees. The cap, including VAT, is 25% in personal injury claims, 35% in employment claims and 50% in other claims.

faq.q: What is After-the-event (ATE) insurance?
faq.a: Insurance bought after a dispute arises that pays the other side's costs, and often your own expenses, if you lose. The premium is frequently deferred and payable only if you win.

faq.q: What is Adverse costs (loser pays)?
faq.a: The rule that the losing party pays part of the winner's legal costs. It is why a no-win-no-fee agreement with your own lawyer does not always mean you risk nothing.

faq.q: What is Litigation funding (third-party funding)?
faq.a: A company that is not a party to the case pays the legal costs in exchange for a share of the money recovered. Funding is usually non-recourse: if the case is lost, you do not repay the funder.

faq.q: What is Cuota litis?
faq.a: An agreement where the lawyer's fee depends on the result, usually a percentage of what is obtained. In Spain the professional ban on it was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2008, so it can be agreed freely in writing.

faq.q: What is Patto di quota lite?
faq.a: An agreement giving the lawyer a share of the asset or sum in dispute. Since 2012 Italian law forbids it again, but a fee calculated as a percentage of the value of the case, agreed in writing in advance, is allowed.

faq.q: What is Erfolgshonorar?
faq.a: A fee that depends on success. It is generally not allowed for lawyers, with exceptions: for example claims of up to 2,000 euros, certain debt collection work, and cases where the client could not otherwise afford to bring the claim.

faq.q: What is Honoraire de résultat?
faq.a: A bonus linked to the result. A fee based only on the result (pacte de quota litis) is not allowed, but a result-based fee can be added to a fixed or hourly fee if it is agreed in writing.

faq.q: What is Success fee?
faq.a: Any fee, or part of a fee, that is payable only if the case succeeds. How it is calculated, and whether it is allowed at all, depends on the country.

faq.q: What is Limitation period?
faq.a: The deadline for starting a claim. Once it has passed the claim is usually barred, so check it early; periods differ by country and type of claim and can be paused or restarted in some situations.

/fees/cfa-vs-dba.t: CFA vs DBA: Which No-Win-No-Fee Agreement Is Better? | JuriMatch
/fees/cfa-vs-dba.d: Conditional fee agreements and damages-based agreements compared: how each is paid, the legal caps, what you pay if you win or lose, and which suits your claim in England and Wales.
/fees/cfa-vs-dba.h1: Conditional fee agreement (CFA) vs Damages-based agreement (DBA)
/fees/cfa-vs-dba.lead: Both mean you pay your own solicitor nothing if you lose. Under a CFA you pay normal fees plus a capped success fee if you win; under a DBA the solicitor takes a capped percentage of your damages instead. Neither covers the other side's costs, which is what ATE insurance is for.
crumbs: Conditional fee agreement (CFA) vs Damages-based agreement (DBA)
facts: What the lawyer gets if you win
Conditional fee agreement (CFA): Normal (base) fees plus a success fee. Damages-based agreement (DBA): An agreed percentage of the damages.
Legal cap

Conditional fee agreement (CFA): Success fee up to 100% of base costs; in personal injury, up to 25% of certain damages. Damages-based agreement (DBA): Including VAT: 25% in personal injury, 35% in employment, 50% in other claims.
Costs paid by the other side

Conditional fee agreement (CFA): Usually cover much of the base fees; the success fee normally comes out of your damages. Damages-based agreement (DBA): Count towards the agreed percentage, so you usually pay the difference from your damages.
If you lose

Conditional fee agreement (CFA): No fee to your solicitor; the other side's costs unless protected or insured. Damages-based agreement (DBA): No fee to your solicitor; the other side's costs unless protected or insured.
Common in
Conditional fee agreement (CFA): Personal injury, professional negligence, commercial claims. Damages-based agreement (DBA): Employment claims and some commercial claims.

faq.q: Is a CFA or a DBA cheaper?
faq.a: It depends on the size of the damages and how much of the costs you recover. With high damages and low costs a CFA is often cheaper; with low recoverable costs a DBA can work out better. Ask the solicitor to model both on your figures.

faq.q: Do I pay anything if I lose under a CFA or DBA?
faq.a: Not to your own solicitor, if the agreement says so. You may still owe disbursements such as court fees and experts, and the other side's costs unless you are protected (for example by QOCS in most personal injury claims) or insured with ATE insurance.

faq.q: Can a solicitor change from a CFA to a DBA mid-case?
faq.a: Only by a new written agreement that you sign. Read how any work already done is treated before agreeing.

/fees/contingency-fee-vs-litigation-fund.t: Contingency Fee vs Litigation Funding: Which Is Right for Your Claim? | JuriMatch
/fees/contingency-fee-vs-litigation-fund.d: Contingency fees and third-party litigation funding compared: who pays the costs, what each takes from a win, typical claim sizes, and what happens if you lose.
/fees/contingency-fee-vs-litigation-fund.lead: With a contingency fee your own lawyer works without being paid unless you recover. With litigation funding a separate company pays the legal costs, and often the risk of the other side's costs, in return for a share of the recovery. Funders usually look for larger claims.
facts: Who carries the cost of the case
Contingency fee: Your lawyer, by working unpaid until the end. Litigation funding: A third-party funder, who pays the lawyers as the case goes.
What they take if you win
Contingency fee: An agreed percentage of the recovery. Litigation funding: A multiple of the money invested or a percentage of the recovery, whichever the contract says.
If you lose
Contingency fee: No lawyer fee; expenses and the other side's costs may still apply. Litigation funding: Nothing to the funder (non-recourse); many funders also cover the other side's costs.
Typical claim size
Contingency fee: From small to large claims. Litigation funding: Usually larger claims; funders often want damages of around ten times the expected costs.
Where it is allowed
Contingency fee: Widely in the US, Canada and others; restricted in many European countries. Litigation funding: Most major jurisdictions, with rules that differ by country.

faq.q: Can I use a contingency fee and litigation funding together?
faq.a: Sometimes. A funder may pay part of the costs while the law firm takes a reduced fee plus a success element. The total taken from your recovery should be set out in writing before you sign.

faq.q: Do I have to repay a litigation funder if I lose?
faq.a: Normally not: most funding is non-recourse, so the funder loses its investment. Check the agreement for exceptions such as misconduct or abandoning the case.

faq.q: Which leaves me more money if I win?
faq.a: It depends on the percentages, the length of the case and the multiple the funder charges. Ask for a worked example at several outcomes and timelines.

/fees/no-win-no-fee-vs-hourly-fees.t: No Win No Fee vs Paying by the Hour: Pros, Cons and Costs | JuriMatch
/fees/no-win-no-fee-vs-hourly-fees.d: No-win-no-fee agreements and hourly billing compared: what you pay if you win or lose, who carries the risk, and when paying by the hour can still make sense.
/fees/no-win-no-fee-vs-hourly-fees.h1: No win, no fee vs Hourly fees
/fees/no-win-no-fee-vs-hourly-fees.lead: Under no win, no fee you pay your own lawyer nothing if you lose, but give up a share of a win. Paying by the hour costs money whatever the outcome, but you keep the whole award. No win, no fee suits claimants who cannot or do not want to fund the risk.
crumbs: No win, no fee vs Hourly fees
facts: If you lose
No win, no fee: No fee to your own lawyer (expenses and the other side's costs may apply). Hourly fees: All your lawyer's fees, plus possibly the other side's costs.
If you win
No win, no fee: A share of the recovery or a success fee. Hourly fees: The fees already paid; you keep the whole award.
Cash needed during the case
No win, no fee: Little or none. Hourly fees: Regular invoices, often from the start.
Who carries the risk
No win, no fee: Mostly the lawyer. Hourly fees: You.
Case selection
No win, no fee: The lawyer only takes cases with good prospects. Hourly fees: The lawyer can act on cases with lower prospects.

faq.q: Is no win no fee really free if I lose?
faq.a: You pay your own lawyer nothing if the agreement says so, but you may still owe expenses such as court fees and experts, and in most countries outside the US the other side's costs. Ask who covers these before signing.

faq.q: Why would a lawyer turn down my case on no win no fee?
faq.a: Because they are taking the risk. Lawyers look at the chances of winning, the amount at stake, whether the other side can pay, and the time it will take.

faq.q: Can I switch from hourly fees to no win no fee?
faq.a: Sometimes, with a new written agreement. A new firm may also take over a case on success terms after reviewing it.

/claims/investment-fraud.t: Lost money to investment fraud? What to do first | JuriMatch
/claims/investment-fraud.d: A practical guide for victims of investment fraud: the first steps to take, the evidence lawyers need, a realistic timeline and how no-win-no-fee recovery works.
/claims/investment-fraud.h1: Lost money to investment fraud? What to do first
/claims/investment-fraud.lead: Investment fraud covers Ponzi schemes, fake funds, unauthorised trading, mis-sold products and advisers who misrepresented risk. The steps you take in the first weeks often decide whether money can still be traced and recovered.

faq.q: Can I get my money back from an investment scam?
faq.a: Sometimes. It depends on whether the money can be traced, whether a solvent party (a bank, a regulated firm or an identifiable individual with assets) is responsible, and how quickly you act. A lawyer can tell you which of these applies to you.

faq.q: Do lawyers take investment fraud cases on a no-win-no-fee basis?
faq.a: Many do, where recovery looks realistic, for example when a regulated entity or insurer is involved, or many investors were affected by the same scheme. Where it is less certain, firms may offer a reduced fee plus a success fee, or refer you to a litigation funder.

faq.q: Should I join a group claim?
faq.a: Group or collective actions can share costs and make funding easier. Check who runs the claim, how fees are taken from any recovery, and whether you can leave.

/claims/crypto-scam.t: Crypto scam recovery: first steps and how lawyers trace funds | JuriMatch
/claims/crypto-scam.d: What to do after a crypto scam: preserve wallet and transaction evidence, report it, avoid recovery scams and understand how lawyers trace and freeze crypto assets.
/claims/crypto-scam.h1: Crypto scam recovery: first steps and how lawyers trace funds
/claims/crypto-scam.lead: Crypto transfers are public on the blockchain, which means funds can sometimes be followed to an exchange where an account holder can be identified. Speed matters: once funds are moved through mixers or off-ramped, options narrow.

faq.q: Can stolen crypto be recovered?
faq.a: Sometimes, if the funds can be traced to an exchange or custodian that can be compelled to freeze and disclose account information. If funds were moved through mixers or to wallets nobody controls identifiably, recovery is much harder.

faq.q: Is there a no-win-no-fee option for crypto fraud?
faq.a: Some firms work on success terms when tracing shows funds at an identifiable exchange. Initial tracing reports often carry a cost, so ask upfront what is included.

faq.q: How do I spot a recovery scam?
faq.a: Unsolicited contact, upfront fees, claims of special access to blockchains or regulators, and pressure to act fast. Legitimate law firms are regulated and can be checked with the local bar or law society.

/claims/property-fraud.h1: Property and off-plan fraud: how to protect your claim
/claims/property-fraud.lead: Property fraud ranges from fake listings and diverted deposits to off-plan developments that never complete and title problems discovered after purchase. Your contracts and payment records are the foundation of any claim.

faq.q: Can I recover a deposit from a developer that went bust?
faq.a: Possibly, if your deposit was protected by a bank guarantee, escrow or insurance, or if directors can be held personally liable. Otherwise you may be an unsecured creditor in the insolvency.

faq.q: Do I need a lawyer in the country where the property is?
faq.a: Usually yes, because property claims are generally governed by local law and heard by local courts.

faq.q: Will a lawyer recover a debt on a no-win-no-fee basis?
faq.a: Many debt-recovery firms work for a percentage of what they collect, particularly for undisputed business debts.

faq.q: Can I claim interest and costs?
faq.a: Many countries allow statutory interest and some recovery costs on late business payments. A lawyer can confirm what applies to your invoice.

faq.q: Can a shareholder dispute be funded?
faq.a: Yes, where the business or stake is valuable enough. Funders and success-fee firms look at what can realistically be recovered or bought out.

faq.q: Will my bank refund a romance scam payment?
faq.a: It depends on your country, how you paid and the bank's rules. Some countries have reimbursement schemes for authorised push-payment fraud. Report it to the bank immediately.

faq.q: Do lawyers take insurance disputes on a no-win-no-fee basis?
faq.a: Often, because the insurer can pay. The main question is whether the policy wording supports your claim.

/claims/professional-negligence.h1: Bad advice from a professional? Claiming for negligence
/claims/professional-negligence.lead: Professionals owe a duty to act with reasonable skill and care. When they fall short and it causes a financial loss, you may have a claim, usually against their professional indemnity insurance.

faq.q: Who pays if I win a professional negligence claim?
faq.a: Usually the professional's indemnity insurer, which is why these claims are often funded on success terms.
